chapter_title: Basic UI Elements and Player Feedback
chapter_summary:
The User Interface (UI) is the direct line of communication between your game and the player. It provides crucial feedback, displays vital information like health, score, or objectives, and allows players to interact with menus and in-game systems. Without a well-designed UI, even the most engaging gameplay can feel opaque and frustrating. Unreal Engine's powerful **UMG (Unreal Motion Graphics) UI Designer** is your primary tool for building these interactive interfaces. UMG is a visual editor that allows you to drag and drop UI elements, arrange them, and then use Blueprints to drive their functionality.

To begin creating a UI, you'll typically start by creating a **Widget Blueprint**. This is a special type of Blueprint that serves as a container for your UI elements, such as a HUD (Heads-Up Display) for in-game information, a pause menu, or an inventory screen. Once inside the Widget Blueprint editor, you'll find the **Palette** panel, which contains a variety of **common UMG widgets**. These include `Text Block` for displaying text, `Image` for displaying textures or sprites, `Progress Bar` for showing values like health or stamina, and `Button` for interactive clickable elements. You drag these widgets onto the `Canvas Panel` (or other layout panels) in the Designer tab and then arrange, size, and style them using the **Details** panel. For instance, you can set the font, color, and text content of a `Text Block`, or the fill color and percentage of a `Progress Bar`.

Displaying your beautifully designed UI on the player's screen involves two main Blueprint nodes: **`Create Widget`** and **`Add to Viewport`**. Typically, this logic is placed in your `Player Controller` or `Game Mode` Blueprint, often on `Event BeginPlay`. The `Create Widget` node takes your Widget Blueprint Class as input and returns a reference to the newly created instance of your UI. This instance is then passed to the `Add to Viewport` node, which makes it visible on the player's screen. It's a common mistake to create a widget but forget to add it to the viewport, leading to a seemingly invisible UI. Remember, `Create Widget` instantiates it, `Add to Viewport` displays it. If you need to remove a UI element, you can use the `Remove from Parent` node on the widget reference.

The real power of UMG comes from its ability to dynamically update UI elements based on game logic. For `Text Blocks` and `Progress Bars`, you can use **Bindings**. In the Details panel of a widget, next to properties like "Text" or "Percent," you'll see a "Bind" button. Clicking this allows you to create a function that will be called every frame to retrieve the current value for that property. For example, you can bind the text of a `Text Block` to a variable in your `Player Character` that holds the player's current score. Or, you can bind the `Percent` of a `Progress Bar` to a `Health` variable, divided by `Max Health`, to show a health bar. This reactive updating ensures your UI always reflects the current state of the game.

For interactive UI elements like `Buttons`, UMG provides **event handling**. In the Details panel of a `Button` widget, under "Events," you'll find events like `On Clicked`, `On Hovered`, and `On Pressed`. Clicking the `+` button next to `On Clicked` will create a corresponding event node in your Widget Blueprint's Event Graph. Here, you can define what happens when the player clicks the button – for example, opening another menu, performing an action, or increasing a score. A common mistake is trying to put all game logic directly into the UI widget. While simple actions are fine, it's generally better practice to have the UI widget call functions on the `Player Controller` or `Game Mode` to perform complex game state changes, keeping the UI itself focused on presentation and input. This separation of concerns makes your UI more maintainable and reusable.

screens.title: Basic UI Elements and Player Feedback
screens.subtitle: Design simple HUDs with UMG, bind data, and handle button input

narration.text: User interfaces are your game's most direct conversation with players. In this chapter you'll learn how UMG, Unreal's visual UI editor, lets you design, display, and update HUD elements like score text, health bars, and interactive buttons. We'll build a Player HUD using a Widget Blueprint, show how to instantiate it at runtime with the Create Widget and Add to Viewport nodes, and connect UI properties back to game variables using Bindings so the HUD stays reactive. You'll also wire a Button using the On Clicked event to change game state, while practicing separation of concerns so your UI stays focused on presentation and input, not heavy game logic. As you move through the hands-on steps, notice how small design decisions—placement, color, and clear feedback—directly affect player understanding. By the end you'll be able to create a working HUD, bind score and health values, and implement a button that increases score. Think about what feedback your game absolutely needs and why timely, accurate UI updates matter for player experience.

keyIdea.text: Build a simple, dynamic HUD with UMG: create widgets, display them with Blueprint nodes, bind properties to game data, and handle button clicks while keeping logic organized.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the purpose of UI and build a basic HUD in Unreal Engine using UMG. You will learn to create Widget Blueprints, add common widgets like Text Blocks, Progress Bars, and Buttons, and place them within layout panels so they appear correctly on screen. You will also know how to show widgets at runtime by using Create Widget and Add to Viewport, and why forgetting Add to Viewport is a common source of invisible UI. You'll practice binding widget properties such as text and percent to game variables so the UI updates automatically, and you'll wire an On Clicked event on a Button to influence game state. Finally, you will apply a separation-of-concerns approach: keep complex game logic in the Player Controller or Game Mode and let Widgets handle presentation and input. These skills make HUDs reliable, maintainable, and reusable across levels and characters.

screens.title: The Role of UI and Player Feedback
screens.subtitle: Why UI is the game's communication channel

narration.text: UI is the direct line between your game systems and the player. It presents essential information like health, score, objectives, and input affordances so players can make informed decisions. A clear UI reduces confusion and supports flow; a confusing UI can make strong gameplay feel opaque. For example, a health bar that accurately reflects damage and heals provides immediate, understandable feedback about risk and survivability. One misconception is that UI is only decorative; in reality it's functional and often central to player experience. Another common mistake is overcrowding: too many elements compete for attention. Instead prioritize vital signals: a concise score display, a health progress bar, and a single clear button for a simple action. Also consider update frequency — using bindings for properties ensures values reflect runtime state without manual per-frame logic. In practice, aim for readability, consistent placement, and clear color semantics: health bars often use green-to-red scales, while important calls to action use contrasting accent colors. Reflect: which single UI element would most improve your current project and why? The Role of UI and Player Feedback means a focused, reactive ui turns raw game data into actionable feedback; it guides player choices and improves clarity and engagement.. In practical terms, why ui is the game's communication channel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Why UI matters
keyIdea.text: A focused, reactive UI turns raw game data into actionable feedback; it guides player choices and improves clarity and engagement.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Role of UI
Definition

UI as feedback

UI surfaces game state to players so they can interpret what's happening and act. Good feedback reduces frustration and clarifies cause and effect.

Concrete example
A health bar that decreases when damage is taken and fills when healed gives immediate survival feedback.
Common mistake
Treating UI as decoration and placing game logic inside widgets leads to tangled Blueprints and brittle behavior.
Key tip
Prioritize one clear feedback channel per player need: health, score, and primary action.
Annotated example
Score Text
Displays current PlayerScore as text like "Score: 20".
Vital
Health Progress Bar
Shows PlayerHealth / PlayerMaxHealth as percent, using binding for automatic updates.
Add Score Button
Triggers an On Clicked event to increment PlayerScore; keep complex state changes in the controller.
Key Takeaway

Design UI to reveal essential information quickly. Use bindings to keep it accurate, and keep game logic outside the widget when possible.

screens.title: UMG and the Widget Blueprint
screens.subtitle: How Widget Blueprints hold presentation and input

narration.text: UMG, Unreal Motion Graphics, is the visual editor you use to compose UI widgets. The central container is a Widget Blueprint, which holds layout panels, visual widgets, and functions for UI behavior. Think of a Widget Blueprint as an object that defines appearance and light input handling; it is not where heavy game state should live. Inside a Widget Blueprint you'll use the Designer tab to drag widgets from the Palette onto a Canvas Panel or other layout containers, then use the Details panel to set text, colors, anchors, and default values. For events and logic, the Event Graph allows simple responses such as a Button's On Clicked. A common architecture pattern is: Player Controller owns game variables and exposes them to the widget; the Widget binds to controller values or calls controller functions on input. This keeps UI reusable across characters or modes. For example, a WBP_PlayerHUD displays score and health but asks the Player Controller for those values via binding functions or casted references. Misconception: putting persistent game variables inside the widget makes reuse harder and risks losing data when widgets are removed. Keep widgets focused and controllers authoritative.

keyIdea.title: UMG role
keyIdea.text: Widget Blueprints define visual presentation and lightweight input handling; keep persistent game state in controllers or game mode for reuse and stability.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Widget Blueprint
Structure
A Widget Blueprint includes Designer, Palette, Hierarchy, Details, and an Event Graph for minimal UI logic. It is a class instance you create at runtime and add to the viewport.
Runtime ownership pattern
Player Controller holds PlayerScore and PlayerHealth → Controller creates widget → Widget binds to controller data or calls controller functions on input.
Designer
Visual layout and style of widgets.
Event Graph
Handles On Clicked and simple UI behavior; avoid complex game logic here.
Example: WBP_PlayerHUD
Designer elements
Canvas Panel containing a Text Block labeled Score, a green Progress Bar, and a Button that reads Add Score.
Event Graph
Button On Clicked: cast to Player Controller → increase PlayerScore by 10 via a controller setter.
Binding pattern
Create binding function for Text or Percent properties to read variables from the Player Controller each frame.
Common-mistake

Storing authoritative game values in widgets makes state fragile; prefer controller-owned variables and bindings.

screens.title: Common UMG Widgets: Text, Image, Progress Bar, Button
screens.subtitle: What each widget does and when to use it

narration.text: UMG ships with common widgets you will use in most HUDs: Text Block, Image, Progress Bar, and Button. A Text Block displays static or dynamic strings. Use it for labels like Score or objective text. For dynamic values, bind the Text property to a function that returns the current value converted to text. An Image shows textures or sprites and is useful for icons, portraits, or decorative elements. A Progress Bar represents a 0-1 percentage; it is ideal for health, stamina, or any value scaled to a maximum. Bind its Percent property to a calculation like PlayerHealth divided by PlayerMaxHealth so it reacts automatically. A Button is a clickable widget; it exposes events such as On Clicked, On Hovered, and On Pressed. Use On Clicked to trigger a controller function or a small UI change. One misconception is to overload a Button with game logic; instead cast to the Player Controller and call a controller function to perform state changes. Practically, combine these widgets: show a Text Block for score, a Progress Bar for health, an Image icon for context, and a Button to accept player input — this small set covers many HUD needs.

keyIdea.title: Widget roles
keyIdea.text: Text Block for labels and dynamic numbers, Image for icons, Progress Bar for 0–1 values, Button for player-initiated events; bind properties for reactivity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Common Widgets
Widgets at a glance
Text Block
Displays text. Bind Text to PlayerScore and prepend 'Score: ' when returning the string from the binding function.
Image
Shows a texture or icon. Use for life icons, ability images, or HUD decoration.
Progress Bar
Shows percentage. Bind Percent to a division result like PlayerHealth / PlayerMaxHealth for automatic updates.
Button
Clickable widget. Use On Clicked to call controller functions or send events; avoid heavy logic inside the widget.
Example combination
WBP_PlayerHUD components
Top-left: Text Block "Score: 0". Below it: green Progress Bar with Percent bound to PlayerHealth / PlayerMaxHealth. Somewhere visible: Button 'Add Score' that increments score via controller.
Key Takeaway

Combine these widgets to give clear numeric and visual feedback; use bindings to keep them synchronized with game state.

screens.title: Create Widget → Add to Viewport
screens.subtitle: Instantiate and display your HUD at runtime

narration.text: To show a Widget Blueprint in a running game you use two nodes: Create Widget and Add to Viewport. Create Widget takes the Widget Class (for example WBP_PlayerHUD) and returns a reference to the instance it created. Add to Viewport takes that reference and makes it visible to the player. A common workflow puts this logic in the Player Controller's Event BeginPlay so each player gets their HUD when the level starts. Remember to store the returned widget instance in a variable like PlayerHUDRef if you plan to call functions or remove it later. A frequent mistake is calling Create Widget but forgetting Add to Viewport — the widget exists but is never visible. To remove a widget, use Remove from Parent on the stored reference. For multiplayer or split-screen, ensure the correct controller runs this logic so each player sees their own HUD. Example sequence: Event BeginPlay → Create Widget(Class: WBP_PlayerHUD) → Promote Return Value to PlayerHUDRef → Add to Viewport(Target: PlayerHUDRef). Finally, test in Play mode and verify the HUD appears as expected. Create Widget → Add to Viewport means create widget instantiates a widget; add to viewport displays it. store the instance if you need to update or remove it later.. In practical terms, instantiate and display your hud at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Display flow
keyIdea.text: Create Widget instantiates a widget; Add to Viewport displays it. Store the instance if you need to update or remove it later.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Create & Display
Node sequence
Event BeginPlay
→ Create Widget (Class = WBP_PlayerHUD)
→ Promote Return Value to variable PlayerHUDRef
→ Add to Viewport (Target = PlayerHUDRef)
Store the widget reference if you need to call functions on it or remove it later with Remove from Parent.
Pitfall

If Add to Viewport is omitted, the widget will be instantiated but never visible.

Example scenario
In your Player Controller, on BeginPlay create WBP_PlayerHUD, save the returned reference to PlayerHUDRef, and call Add to Viewport. Later you can call Remove from Parent on PlayerHUDRef when the HUD is no longer needed, for example on level end.
Key Takeaway

Always pair Create Widget with Add to Viewport and keep a reference to the widget if you will update or remove it later.

screens.title: Bindings: Keeping UI Reactive
screens.subtitle: Bind Text and Percent to game variables

narration.text: Bindings connect widget properties to functions that provide values at runtime, letting UI update reactively. To bind a Text Block's text or a Progress Bar's percent, click Bind in the Details panel next to the property and create a binding function. Inside that function you typically get a reference to the Player Controller, cast it to your controller class, and read variables like PlayerScore or PlayerHealth. For a health bar, return PlayerHealth divided by PlayerMaxHealth to produce a 0-1 Percent value. For a score text binding, get PlayerScore, convert it to text and prepend descriptive text such as 'Score: '. Bindings are favored over manually updating values on Event Tick because they centralize logic and let UMG optimize updates. A common misconception is that bindings always run every frame; they are called when the UI needs the value, and their overhead is less than ad-hoc per-frame logic cluttering the widget's Event Graph. Example: create a Progress Bar binding that divides PlayerHealth by PlayerMaxHealth and returns percent. Test by modifying PlayerHealth in the controller and watching the bar update. Bindings: Keeping UI Reactive means bindings centralize and optimize property updates for text and percent, keeping ui accurate without per-frame manual updates.. In practical terms, bind text and percent to game variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Binding benefit
keyIdea.text: Bindings centralize and optimize property updates for text and percent, keeping UI accurate without per-frame manual updates.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Bindings
How to bind
  1. Select the widget (Text Block or Progress Bar).
  2. In Details, click Bind next to Text or Percent and choose Create Binding.
  3. In the binding function, get Player Controller, cast to your controller class, access PlayerScore or PlayerHealth.
  4. Return the proper type: Text for Text Block, float 0-1 for Percent.
Key Tip

For percent bindings divide current by max to produce a 0-1 value, and convert numbers to text for display bindings.

Binding example
// Pseudocode for a binding function in the widget
Get Player Controller
Cast to ThirdPersonPlayerController
Get PlayerHealth
Get PlayerMaxHealth
Return PlayerHealth / PlayerMaxHealth  // float 0-1 for Percent
This function is attached to the Progress Bar's Percent property and ensures the bar reflects the controller's health values automatically.
Misconception

Avoid writing manual Event Tick updates for UI properties; use bindings to keep logic focused and efficient.

screens.title: Buttons and Event Handling
screens.subtitle: Use On Clicked to trigger actions without bloating the widget

narration.text: Buttons expose events such as On Clicked, On Hovered, and On Pressed in the Details panel. When you click the plus next to On Clicked, UMG creates an event node in the widget's Event Graph. From there you can handle simple UI-only responses, but best practice is to forward actions to the Player Controller or Game Mode for significant game-state changes. For example, in WBP_PlayerHUD the Add Score button's On Clicked can cast to the Player Controller and call a function there to increase PlayerScore by 10. This keeps the widget free of specialized game logic and makes it reusable. One common error is incrementing controller variables directly without casting properly, which leads to null references if the cast fails. Another mistake is placing complex algorithms inside On Clicked handlers; instead, call a named controller function like IncrementScore and test it in isolation. When testing, ensure the button visually responds on click and that the score text binding shows the changed value. This pattern gives you a clear separation: the widget handles input, the controller owns state changes. Buttons and Event Handling means use on clicked to forward user actions to controller functions; keep widgets lean and controllers authoritative for game state changes.. In practical terms, use on clicked to trigger actions without bloating the widget. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Button best practice
keyIdea.text: Use On Clicked to forward user actions to controller functions; keep widgets lean and controllers authoritative for game state changes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Buttons & Events
On Clicked flow
// In WBP_PlayerHUD Event Graph
OnClicked (AddScoreButton)
→ Get Player Controller
→ Cast To ThirdPersonPlayerController
→ Call IncrementScore(Amount = 10)
IncrementScore is a controller function that updates PlayerScore and keeps game state centralized.
Testing & Common mistakes
  • Ensure the cast to your controller succeeds; otherwise the function call will fail.
  • Do not place heavy gameplay logic inside the widget's Event Graph.
  • Verify the binding updates the visible text after the controller changes the value.
Pro tip

Name your controller functions with clear verbs like IncrementScore so the widget calls read clearly in the Event Graph.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create WBP_PlayerHUD
screens.subtitle: Designer steps to place Score, Health Bar, and Add Score button

narration.text: Let's build the WBP_PlayerHUD step by step. First, create a Widget Blueprint in the Content Browser and name it WBP_PlayerHUD. Open it and ensure a Canvas Panel is present as the root. Drag a Text Block onto the Canvas and set its text to 'Score: 0' and a readable font size. Anchor it to the top-left so it stays in a consistent position on different resolutions. Next, add a Progress Bar below the score and set its Fill Color to a green tint; this will become the health bar. Finally, add a Button somewhere convenient and place a child Text Block inside the Button labeled 'Add Score'. Style the button to contrast with the background so it reads as clickable. Save the widget. These visual steps establish the presentation layer. A frequent oversight is not adjusting anchors or scale, which makes UI shift across resolutions. Test your layout in different viewport sizes in the Designer tab to ensure readability. This exercise prepares the widget for runtime instantiation and binding in the next steps. Hands-on: Create WBP_PlayerHUD means create wbp_playerhud with anchored score text, a green progress bar for health, and a clearly styled add score button; test layout across viewports.. In practical terms, designer steps to place score, health bar, and add score button. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Create WBP_PlayerHUD
Designer actions
  1. Create Widget Blueprint → WBP_PlayerHUD.
  2. Confirm Canvas Panel root is present.
  3. Drag Text Block, set text to 'Score: 0', anchor top-left.
  4. Add Progress Bar, set Fill Color to green, position below score.
  5. Add Button, add child Text 'Add Score', style for contrast.
Layout notes
Use anchors to lock UI to corners and check scale with different safe-zone settings. Avoid placing critical info at the absolute edges where it can be cropped on some displays.
Quick test
Open the Designer viewport size selector and check small, medium, and large resolutions to confirm element positions and text legibility.
Key Takeaway

Careful anchors and readable fonts make a HUD usable across resolutions; the visual design should support immediate comprehension.

screens.title: Player Controller: Create Widget & Variables
screens.subtitle: Add HUD on BeginPlay and own score/health variables

narration.text: Now switch to the Player Controller Blueprint to display the HUD and own game variables. In your controller's Event BeginPlay add Create Widget and set Class to WBP_PlayerHUD. Promote the Return Value to a variable called PlayerHUDRef and then connect Add to Viewport with the Return Value as Target. Next create three Float variables in the controller: PlayerScore (default 0), PlayerHealth (default 100), and PlayerMaxHealth (default 100). Storing these in the controller keeps them authoritative and accessible to the HUD via binding. When the widget binds to controller values it will read the latest PlayerScore and PlayerHealth from the controller, providing accurate feedback. If you plan to adjust these variables from other systems, expose controller functions like IncrementScore or SetHealth so widgets or other Blueprints can call them safely. A common pitfall is forgetting to make the reference visible to the widget during binding; ensure bindings cast to the correct controller class. After wiring these nodes, play the level and verify the HUD displays correctly and the variables exist on the controller instance. Player Controller: Create Widget & Variables means place playerscore and playerhealth in the player controller, create the widget on beginplay, and save the widget reference for later updates or removal.. In practical terms, add hud on beginplay and own score/health variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Place PlayerScore and PlayerHealth in the Player Controller, create the widget on BeginPlay, and save the widget reference for later updates or removal.

screens.title: Bindings and Button Implementation
screens.subtitle: Wire the Score binding, Health percent, and Add Score button

narration.text: Finish the HUD by creating bindings and the Add Score event. In WBP_PlayerHUD select the Score Text Block and click Bind next to Text → Create Binding. In that function get the Player Controller, cast to your controller class, get PlayerScore, convert the float to text and prepend 'Score: '. For the Progress Bar, create a Percent binding: get PlayerController, cast, get PlayerHealth and PlayerMaxHealth, divide health by max health and return the result. For the Add Score button, in the Event Graph click the plus next to On Clicked, then in the new event get Player Controller, cast and call a controller function such as IncrementScore or directly Get PlayerScore, add 10 and Set PlayerScore. Prefer adding a controller function for clarity and reuse. After wiring, play the level and click Add Score — the binding should update the displayed score immediately. If it doesn't, check that the widget instance was created and added to the viewport and that the casted controller class matches your game controller. This completes the reactive HUD loop. narration.text: When your HUD doesn't behave as expected, three common issues usually explain it: you created the widget but didn't add it to the viewport, bindings fail due to wrong casts, or the widget holds state it shouldn't. If the HUD is invisible, check that Create Widget's Return Value is passed to Add to Viewport and that the code runs (Event BeginPlay can be skipped if not connected). For failed bindings, open the binding function and confirm you cast to the correct Player Controller class; wrong casts return null and yield default values. When UI values feel stale, ensure you're reading live controller variables and not local widget copies; prefer controller-owned variables and binding reads. Use Print String nodes or breakpoints in Blueprints to confirm event execution order. Also test across windows sizes to ensure anchors and safe zones keep elements visible. A pro tip: expose small controller functions like IncrementScore so widgets call named behaviors; this makes debugging simpler because you can place logs or breakpoints inside controller functions where the authoritative state changes occur. Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Debugging Tips
Issue: Invisible Widget
Confirm Create Widget is followed by Add to Viewport and that the Event BeginPlay executes. Use Print String to verify execution.
Issue: Failed Casts
Open binding functions and check your Cast To node's target class. If the wrong controller class is used the binding will return defaults.
Issue: Stale UI
Keep game state in the controller. If widgets store values locally they can become out of sync when the controller changes state elsewhere.
Pro tip
Use small controller functions like IncrementScore so you can add logging inside controller code and isolate problems away from the widget.

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas. First: UI is the player's communication channel; a clear HUD improves player understanding and responsiveness. Second: Widget Blueprints in UMG define presentation and handle light input, while the Player Controller or Game Mode should hold authoritative game state like scores and health. Third: Use Create Widget and Add to Viewport to display widgets at runtime, and store the returned instance for later updates or removal. Fourth: Bindings let you attach a widget property to a function that returns a live value — use bindings for Text and Percent properties so the HUD reflects controller variables. Fifth: Buttons expose On Clicked events; let the widget forward actions to controller functions instead of embedding heavy logic inside the widget. Keep widgets focused on display and input, and controllers focused on state and behavior. These habits make your UI robust, reusable, and easy to debug.
